operations.before: Suppose $\ker M=\{0\}$. By [F1], $\operatorname{rank}(M)=n$; by [F2] the image of $M$ has dimension $n$ in the $n$-dimensional space $\mathbb C^n$, so $M$ is surjective. It is also injective by the supposition, hence invertible.

operations.before: Apply [F5] to obtain orthonormal bases $z_1,z_2$ of $X$ and $q_1,q_2$ of $Y$, choosing $q_1,q_2$ by Gram–Schmidt on $Bz_1,Bz_2$. Since the two images are independent, the leading matrix $B_{11}=Q_1^TBZ_1$ is upper triangular with nonzero diagonal and hence invertible. Extend these bases by orthonormal bases of $Y^\perp$ and $X^\perp$ using [F6]. In these full bases, the first two columns of both transformed matrices are supported in the first two rows. Let $P$ be the invertible change-of-basis matrix from $(x,y)$ to $(z_1,z_2)$. The equations in step 2.2 give $A[z_1\ z_2]=B[z_1\ z_2]C$, where $C=P^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\-b&a\end{pmatrix}P$. Thus the leading blocks satisfy $A_{11}=B_{11}C$, and $C$ is similar to $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\-b&a\end{pmatrix}$. Consequently $\det(A_{11}-\mu B_{11}) =\det(B_{11})\det(C-\mu I) =\det(B_{11})\bigl((a-\mu)^2+b^2\bigr)$ is a nonzero polynomial with roots $a\pm ib$.
operations.after: Apply [F5] to obtain orthonormal bases $z_1,z_2$ of $X$ and $q_1,q_2$ of $Y$, choosing $q_1,q_2$ by Gram–Schmidt on $Bz_1,Bz_2$. The restriction $B|_X:X\to Y$ sends a basis to the independent pair $Bz_1,Bz_2$ and is therefore an isomorphism. Its matrix in these bases is $B_{11}=Q_1^TBZ_1$, so $B_{11}$ is invertible and [F7] gives $\det(B_{11})\ne0$; the Gram–Schmidt choice makes this matrix upper triangular. Extend these bases by orthonormal bases of $Y^\perp$ and $X^\perp$ using [F6]. In these full bases, the first two columns of both transformed matrices are supported in the first two rows. Let $P$ be the invertible change-of-basis matrix from $(x,y)$ to $(z_1,z_2)$. The equations in step 2.2 give $A[z_1\ z_2]=B[z_1\ z_2]C$, where $C=P^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\-b&a\end{pmatrix}P$. Thus the leading blocks satisfy $A_{11}=B_{11}C$, and $C$ is similar to $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\-b&a\end{pmatrix}$. Consequently $\det(A_{11}-\mu B_{11}) =\det(B_{11})\det(C-\mu I) =\det(B_{11})\bigl((a-\mu)^2+b^2\bigr)$ is a nonzero polynomial with roots $a\pm ib$.

operations.before:
Input $A,B\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, with
$\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. All transformations here are exact.
Let $Q=Z=I_n$.

Use a left Givens factor $L(a,b)$ that sends the column pair $(a,b)^T$ to
$(\gamma,0)^T$, with $|\gamma|=(|a|^2+|b|^2)^{1/2}$; if $a=b=0$, use the
identity. Use a right Givens factor $R(a,b)$ that sends the row pair $(a,b)$ to
$(0,\eta)$, with $|\eta|=(|a|^2+|b|^2)^{1/2}$; if $a=b=0$, use the identity.
These factors are obtained from
[[def-real-and-complex-givens-transformations]] and are orthogonal over
$\mathbb R$ or unitary over $\mathbb C$.

1. Triangularise $B$ by left rotations. For $j=1,\ldots,n$ and, in descending
order, $i=n,n-1,\ldots,j+1$, set
$$L=L(B_{i-1,j},B_{i,j}),\quad A\leftarrow LA,\quad B\leftarrow LB, \quad Q\leftarrow QL^*.$$

2. Reduce $A$ to upper Hessenberg form while restoring triangularity of $B$.
For $j=1,\ldots,n-2$ and, in descending order, $i=n,n-1,\ldots,j+2$, set
$$L=L(A_{i-1,j},A_{i,j}),\quad A\leftarrow LA,\quad B\leftarrow LB, \quad Q\leftarrow QL^*,$$
then set
$$R=R(B_{i,i-1},B_{i,i}),\quad A\leftarrow AR,\quad B\leftarrow BR, \quad Z\leftarrow ZR.$$

Return $Q,Z,H=A,T=B$, where $H$ is upper Hessenberg and $T$ is upper
triangular in the senses of
[[def-upper-hessenberg-and-real-symmetric-tridiagonal-matrices]] and
[[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]]. The outputs are represented by the exact products of
the recorded Givens factors; no dense rounded factor is asserted unitary.
operations.after:
Input $A,B\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, with
$\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. All transformations here are exact.
Let $Q=Z=I_n$.

For a target pair $(a,b)$, define the left factor $L(a,b)$ deterministically. Use $I_2$ if $a=b=0$. Otherwise put $r=(|a|^2+|b|^2)^{1/2}$ and $L=\begin{pmatrix}c&s\\-\overline s&c\end{pmatrix}$. Over $\mathbb R$, take $c=a/r$, $s=b/r$. Over $\mathbb C$, if $a=0$ take $c=0$, $s=\overline b/|b|$; otherwise take $\phi=a/|a|$, $c=|a|/r$, $s=\phi\overline b/r$. Thus $L(a,b)(a,b)^T=(\gamma,0)^T$ with $|\gamma|=r$. Set $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and define the right factor
$$R(a,b)=J L(\overline b,\overline a)^*J.$$
Then $(a,b)R(a,b)=(0,\eta)$ with $|\eta|=r$; the zero pair again uses identity. These factors are real orthogonal over $\mathbb R$ or unitary over $\mathbb C$, as direct multiplication shows in [[thm-householder-reflectors-and-givens-transformations-are-unitary-and-annihilate-targeted-entries]]; the right identity follows by taking adjoints of the left annihilation of $(\overline b,\overline a)^T$ and reversing the coordinates. Use their identity embeddings on the two rows or columns specified by each step below.
1. Triangularise $B$ by left rotations. For $j=1,\ldots,n$ and, in descending
order, $i=n,n-1,\ldots,j+1$, set
$$L=L(B_{i-1,j},B_{i,j}),\quad A\leftarrow LA,\quad B\leftarrow LB, \quad Q\leftarrow QL^*.$$

2. Reduce $A$ to upper Hessenberg form while restoring triangularity of $B$.
For $j=1,\ldots,n-2$ and, in descending order, $i=n,n-1,\ldots,j+2$, set
$$L=L(A_{i-1,j},A_{i,j}),\quad A\leftarrow LA,\quad B\leftarrow LB, \quad Q\leftarrow QL^*,$$
then set
$$R=R(B_{i,i-1},B_{i,i}),\quad A\leftarrow AR,\quad B\leftarrow BR, \quad Z\leftarrow ZR.$$

Return $Q,Z,H=A,T=B$, where $H$ is upper Hessenberg and $T$ is upper
triangular in the senses of
[[def-upper-hessenberg-and-real-symmetric-tridiagonal-matrices]] and
[[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]]. The outputs are represented by the exact products of
the recorded Givens factors; no dense rounded factor is asserted unitary.
